strengths: The paper identifies a useful and underexplored target for reward-free/offline representation learning: approximating minimum action distance from state-only trajectories, including asymmetric reachability structure. This is a meaningful problem for goal-conditioned RL and planning.

The proposed simple ReLU-based quasimetric is technically clean, computationally lightweight, and accompanied by basic proofs of triangle inequality/positive homogeneity. The MadDist objective is also easy to understand and implement.

The evaluation is broader than many representation-learning papers: it includes discrete and continuous domains, stochastic/noisy observations, asymmetric transitions, OGBench PointMaze/AntMaze variants, multiple baselines, ablations over latent size/quasimetric/dataset size, and a downstream planning experiment.
Presentation is generally clear. The paper defines MAD, motivates why symmetry is limiting, describes losses and hyperparameters, and provides appendices with environment and implementation details.
weaknesses: The central claim that MAD can be learned from trajectories of arbitrary quality and in a policy-agnostic way is not fully supported. Observed trajectory gaps provide only upper bounds on MAD, and missing action alternatives or poor coverage can make these bounds loose. The method cannot identify unobserved one-step transitions from state-only data, so the true MAD of the underlying MDP is generally not identifiable without strong coverage assumptions.

The learning objective is heuristic relative to the stated constrained optimization problem. MadDist explicitly pulls distances toward trajectory time gaps, although these can be much larger than the minimum action distance under another policy. The contrastive term pushes random pairs apart, which may conflict with true short MAD pairs that are not co-observed. The paper does not provide theory or diagnostics characterizing when the learned distances are consistent.

The ground-truth MAD used in continuous physics domains appears only approximate and in some cases mismatched to the MDP state. For PointMaze/AntMaze, shortest paths on a discretized maze layout ignore velocities, torque dynamics, contacts, and high-dimensional body state, while the learned model consumes full observations. This weakens claims that the method accurately recovers true MAD in continuous-control MDPs.

The downstream planning evaluation is not entirely clean. It uses the true simulator and, for AntMaze, selects trajectory segments from the navigate dataset because random action sampling is ineffective. This evaluates the learned metric in a helpful heuristic pipeline, but it mixes access assumptions and does not isolate whether the method would support realistic offline goal-conditioned control.

Empirical comparisons are incomplete for acceptance-level confidence. Only QRL and Hilbert are used as main baselines; there is limited comparison to simpler alternatives such as graph shortest paths on observed transitions, temporal contrastive methods, successor-feature distances, or direct supervised baselines using trajectory indices. Statistical reporting is modest, with only three seeds for main results and large variances in some OGBench planning entries.

The paper overstates some conclusions. TDMadDist is presented as a novel algorithm, but the main results show it often underperforms MadDist and sometimes QRL; the discussion still frames it quite positively. Claims of robustness to stochasticity and arbitrary data quality need more stress tests under systematically degraded coverage and rare transitions.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and compute are listed, but the manuscript does not clearly state whether code, datasets, exact seeds, environment implementations, or ground-truth MAD computation scripts will be released. Some hyperparameter entries are ranges without specifying selection protocol.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The conclusion briefly mentions stochastic shortest-path alternatives, but the manuscript does not sufficiently discuss identifiability limits, coverage dependence, approximate ground truth in continuous domains, or failure modes when MAD is an unsafe or misleading planning heuristic.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful problem: learning directed state distances from offline trajectories could be useful for goal-conditioned RL, planning heuristics, and representation learning, especially in environments with irreversible dynamics.

The MAD formulation as a shortest-path/quasimetric object is intuitive, and the proposed ReLU-based quasimetric is simple, computationally cheap, and accompanied by a basic triangle-inequality argument.

The evaluation attempts to include asymmetric, stochastic, noisy-observation, discrete, and continuous-control environments, and reports several distance-quality metrics plus a downstream planning experiment rather than only qualitative embeddings.
weaknesses: The central identifiability claim is not supported. MAD is defined over the support of the MDP transition kernel, but the algorithms only observe state trajectories from a behavior policy. Without actions or sufficient transition coverage, unseen one-step edges and shorter paths are not identifiable. The paper repeatedly claims policy agnosticism, arbitrary data quality, and trajectory stitching, but provides no theorem, sample-complexity analysis, or convincing experiment showing recovery under missing coverage.

The learning objective is weakly justified and can be wrong under suboptimal trajectories. The main loss pushes learned distances toward j-i along observed trajectories, which is only an upper bound on MAD and may be very loose. The contrastive term pushes random pairs apart, which does not correspond to shortest-path recovery. TDMadDist bootstraps along observed successors but still lacks a minimization over possible actions/successors, so it does not resolve the core mismatch.

The experiments do not convincingly validate the strong claims. Many environments have ground-truth MAD only by construction or approximation; for PointMaze/AntMaze the reported “ground truth” is computed on a discretized maze layout and ignores velocities, actuation limits, contacts, and high-dimensional ant dynamics, so it is not clearly the true minimum action distance of the stated MDP.

The downstream planning evaluation is heavily confounded. PointMaze uses the true simulator for MPC rollouts, while AntMaze selects trajectory segments from a navigate dataset because random action sampling fails. This evaluates a privileged planner/dataset retrieval procedure, not a generally useful learned representation for offline RL. The table reports high variance and only a small number of seeds/tasks.

Baselines and ablations are insufficient for acceptance. The comparison is mainly QRL and Hilbert; there is no simple graph shortest-path baseline on observed transitions, kNN/geodesic baseline, symmetric version with matched capacity, or behavior-policy temporal-distance baseline. Hyperparameter selection is unclear, and model capacities differ substantially, e.g. MadDist uses a 512-dimensional latent space while Hilbert uses 32 dimensions.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript gives some hyperparameters, but lacks pseudocode, code availability, dataset construction details, exact train/evaluation splits, ground-truth distance computation procedures, and selection protocols for values listed as alternatives such as wr and dmax.

Presentation has several inconsistencies and overstatements. For example, NoisyGridWorld dynamics differ between the main text and appendix, the text claims comprehensive known MAD values where some are approximations, and the conclusion says downstream incorporation remains future work despite presenting a planning experiment. The limitations discussion misses the most important limitations: coverage, identifiability, approximation of continuous-domain MAD, and dependence on privileged planning machinery.

The paper has no apparent major ethical risks, but it also does not meaningfully discuss limitations or possible misuse/failure modes of learned distance heuristics in safety-critical decision-making.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: learning Minimum Action Distance representations from state-only trajectories without rewards or actions. The framing is clear, and the distinction between MAD, temporal distance, stochastic shortest path, and symmetric representation-learning objectives is useful.

The proposed MadDist objective is simple and practical. Combining trajectory-based upper-bound supervision, a constraint penalty, and an asymmetric quasimetric embedding is a coherent way to target directed reachability structure while avoiding explicit all-pairs shortest-path computation.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many representation-learning papers: it covers deterministic and stochastic settings, discrete and continuous state spaces, noisy observations, asymmetric dynamics, and OGBench PointMaze/AntMaze variants. The use of environments with known or approximated ground-truth MAD enables direct quantitative evaluation rather than only downstream proxy metrics.

Results are consistently favorable for MadDist. The paper reports strong Pearson/Spearman correlations, lower ratio-CV, and substantially better planning success than QRL and Hilbert baselines in many OGBench settings, including stitch-style datasets where trajectory composition matters.

The ablations are helpful. The paper studies latent dimensionality, dataset size, and quasimetric choice, and the simple ReLU-based quasimetric appears surprisingly effective relative to IQE and WideNorm variants.

Presentation is generally clear. Definitions, objectives, experimental setup, and appendices are readable, and the paper provides enough hyperparameter and implementation detail for a reasonable reproduction attempt.
weaknesses: The method’s central claims require stronger qualification around coverage. From state-only trajectories, unobserved transitions cannot be inferred in general, and trajectory distances are only upper bounds on MAD. The paper sometimes describes the method as policy-agnostic or usable with datasets of any quality, but the objective can overestimate distances when the behavior policy does not reveal short paths or adequate transition support.

The theoretical treatment is limited. The uniqueness proof is for an idealized finite graph-style formulation and does not fully address disconnected states, infinite distances, continuous state spaces, approximation error, or identifiability from sampled trajectories. The learning objectives are plausible relaxations but are not shown to consistently recover MAD under explicit assumptions.

The proposed simple quasimetric is useful empirically but mathematically modest. It is essentially a ReLU-positive-difference aggregation, and depending on terminology it lacks separation because the distance can be zero for distinct ordered embeddings. The paper should be more precise about whether it is using a quasimetric, hemimetric, or preorder-style distance.

The downstream planning evaluation is encouraging but not fully representative of offline RL utility. The planner uses the true environment simulator for rollouts, and for AntMaze it samples trajectory segments from the dataset rather than learning a deployable policy or model. This isolates the metric but limits the strength of claims about practical goal-conditioned RL performance.

Baseline comparison details leave some uncertainty. QRL and Hilbert are strong relevant choices, but the paper does not provide enough evidence that they were tuned as carefully as the proposed method across all environments, and some Hilbert results are extremely poor, which raises questions about implementation or adaptation to this evaluation protocol.

Statistical evidence is somewhat thin. Main experiments use three seeds in places, while some ablations use five, and the figures mainly show min/max bands. Confidence intervals, significance tests, and tabulated full numerical results would make the empirical conclusions more convincing.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics discussion. The risks are not severe compared with human-facing applications, but the authors should more explicitly discuss failure under partial coverage, stochastic transitions with rare support events, continuous-state discretization artifacts, computational scaling, and possible misuse of learned distance heuristics in safety-critical control.

strengths: The paper tackles a useful problem: learning minimum-action-distance representations from reward-free, action-free state trajectories, including asymmetric distances. This is a meaningful direction for goal-conditioned RL, planning heuristics, and state abstraction.

The formulation connecting MAD to a constrained shortest-path/quasimetric optimization problem is clear and mostly well motivated. The proposed simple ReLU-based quasimetric is attractive because it is easy to implement, computationally cheap, and empirically competitive with IQE/WideNorm variants.

The empirical suite is broader than is typical for this topic, covering discrete grids, noisy observations, stochastic transitions, asymmetric mechanisms, PointMaze/AntMaze, and downstream planning. Reporting Pearson, Spearman, ratio CV, five seeds, and ablations over latent size, quasimetric choice, dataset size, constraint horizon, and contrastive weight strengthens the empirical story.
The paper includes substantial implementation details and baseline hyperparameters, making the experimental setup more understandable than many representation-learning submissions.
weaknesses: A central soundness issue is identifiability from arbitrary state-only trajectories. The loss treats trajectory gaps j-i as targets or upper-bound constraints, but these are generally only behavior-policy path lengths, not shortest-path MAD values. Without strong coverage assumptions, shortest paths may be absent, suboptimal trajectories may dominate, and the contrastive term can actively push distances away from the true MAD. The paper repeatedly claims policy agnosticism and learning from data of any quality, but does not provide theoretical or empirical evidence sufficient to support those claims.

The continuous-control ground truth is questionable. For PointMaze/AntMaze, the reported MAD is approximated by discretizing maze layout and computing grid shortest paths, apparently ignoring velocities, contacts, torque limits, ant locomotion dynamics, and the 29-dimensional state. This may evaluate correlation with maze geodesic distance rather than the actual minimum number of environment actions in the MDP, weakening the core claim that the learned metric approximates true MAD.

The downstream planning evaluation is only a controlled diagnostic and relies on the true simulator. For AntMaze, candidate actions/segments are selected from dataset trajectory segments using the learned distance, which differs substantially from a deployable planner and can entangle dataset coverage with metric quality. The results are promising but do not fully establish usefulness for practical RL pipelines.

Baseline comparison raises some concerns. Some baselines are not naturally designed for the exact same action-free/MAD setting, and the QRL objective as written appears to penalize relu(d+1)^2 for transitions, which would be unusual and may indicate either a typo or an implementation mismatch. The paper should more carefully justify fairness, tuning budget, and whether baseline adaptations preserve the intended algorithms.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code availability line is blank, environment construction details are lengthy but not sufficient to exactly reproduce datasets and ground-truth computation, and some key experimental choices are deferred to figures without numeric tables. The lack of released code is a material weakness given the number of custom environments and baseline adaptations.

The limitations discussion is fairly brief and does not squarely address the main failure modes: missing transition support, partial observability/noisy observations breaking state identity, disconnected datasets, behavior-policy bias, and mismatch between MAD and expected/stochastic shortest-path objectives. Ethics and broader impacts are not meaningfully discussed, though the work does not appear to raise unusual ethical risks.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful problem: learning action-free state distances that can support goal-conditioned RL and planning, especially when the true distance is asymmetric.
The idea of using quasimetrics for MAD is appropriate, and the simple ReLU-based asymmetric distance is computationally attractive compared with heavier IQE-style constructions.

The evaluation attempts to cover several relevant regimes, including asymmetric gridworlds, stochastic/noisy observations, continuous maze domains, and downstream planning. The appendices provide many hyperparameters and ablations.
weaknesses: The central claim is not identifiable from the stated data. State-only trajectories provide upper bounds along behavior-generated paths, not the minimum action distance over all actions. If the behavior policy takes suboptimal paths or omits transitions, the proposed losses will generally learn behavior/path distances or arbitrary separations, not MAD. This directly contradicts claims of being policy-agnostic and usable with datasets of any quality.

The learning objective is poorly justified. The main term explicitly regresses learned distances to j-i, although j-i is only an upper bound and can be much larger than MAD. The contrastive term pushes random pairs toward an arbitrary dmax and can overestimate reachable pairs. The constraint loss only covers observed trajectory pairs, not the one-step reachability relation needed by the MAD characterization.

The theoretical formulation has serious gaps. The LP-style uniqueness result ignores unreachable pairs/infinite distances and is not well-defined for continuous state spaces where sums over S^2 are used. The constraints also omit important domain conditions such as nonnegativity, and the transition from the exact constrained problem to the learned objective is a heuristic rather than a sound relaxation with guarantees.

The reported ground-truth MAD is questionable for the continuous control benchmarks. For PointMaze and especially AntMaze, the paper approximates MAD using a maze grid and largely ignores velocities, robot configuration, locomotion dynamics, and continuous action feasibility. Thus the experiments may evaluate correlation with a hand-designed maze heuristic rather than true minimum action distance in the MDP.

The downstream planning evaluation is not clean evidence for the representation. It uses the true simulator and, for AntMaze, selects trajectory segments from a navigate dataset rather than sampling actions normally. This setup may reflect dataset retrieval and simulator access more than a practically useful learned distance, and it is not comparable to standard offline goal-conditioned RL pipelines.

Baseline treatment raises concerns. The QRL objective is presented with a locality penalty relu(d+1)^2, which appears inconsistent with enforcing small one-step distances and may be a typo or flawed implementation. Baselines are not clearly tuned to the same degree as the proposed method, and most ablations are only on CliffWalking or selected AntMaze settings.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a main-track empirical paper. The code availability field is blank, many key implementation details for sampling pairs, evaluation pair sets, preprocessing, and benchmark construction are underspecified, and much of the quantitative evidence is only in figures without precise numerical tables.

The paper overstates its conclusions. Phrases such as learning from arbitrary-quality data, recovering MAD under stochasticity, and decisively outperforming all baselines are stronger than what the objective and experiments support.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The paper briefly notes planner limitations and future work, but does not honestly discuss the core identifiability issue, dependence on coverage, approximate ground truth in continuous domains, simulator assumptions, or potential misuse/failure modes of learned heuristics.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and useful problem: learning minimum-action-distance representations from state-only offline trajectories, including asymmetric environments where Euclidean or symmetric latent distances are structurally inadequate.

The formulation connecting MAD to shortest paths and quasimetric embeddings is intuitive, and the proposed simple ReLU-based quasimetric is appealingly lightweight compared with IQE-style constructions.

The empirical suite is broader than usual for this topic, covering discrete and continuous observations, stochasticity, noisy observations, asymmetric transitions, PointMaze/AntMaze variants, and downstream planning diagnostics.

The evaluation includes relevant baselines such as QRL, PlanDist, PlanDist with the proposed quasimetric, and Hilbert representations, plus ablations over latent dimension, quasimetric choice, dataset size, contrastive weight, and constraint horizon.

The results are consistently favorable for MadDist, especially in asymmetric and long-horizon settings, and the downstream random-shooting planning experiment provides useful evidence that the learned distances can guide behavior rather than only correlate with held-out distances.
weaknesses: The central learning objective is only a heuristic relaxation of the MAD optimization problem. It trains trajectory pairs to match the observed temporal separation j-i even though this is only an upper bound and may be much larger than the true MAD; the paper does not sufficiently analyze when this bias disappears or when it can lead to systematic overestimation.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence supports. In particular, the manuscript says the approach is agnostic to data-collection policy and works with datasets of any quality or fragmented trajectories, but recovery of MAD from state-only data necessarily depends on transition coverage. The dataset-size ablation supports graceful degradation, but not identifiability under arbitrary missing transitions.

The theoretical treatment ignores or underdevelops unreachable state pairs and infinite distances. The uniqueness proof and all-pairs objective assume finite shortest paths, but many directed MDPs or offline datasets may contain disconnected components; this matters directly for asymmetric reachability.

Ground-truth MAD in the continuous-control environments is approximated by grid shortest paths through the maze layout, often ignoring velocity, actuation limits, ant locomotion dynamics, and stochastic contact effects. This is a useful proxy, but the paper sometimes presents it as true MAD, which weakens the soundness of the strongest empirical claims.

The downstream planning evaluation is informative but limited. It uses the true simulator, and for AntMaze selects trajectory segments from the dataset rather than testing a full offline RL or deployable planner. Thus it isolates metric quality, but does not fully establish practical downstream RL usefulness.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code availability field is blank, implementation details are helpful but not enough to reproduce datasets, sampling procedures, exact train/test splits, and evaluation pair generation. Public code or a detailed artifact would be important for acceptance-level reproducibility.

The presentation is generally clear, but some experimental figures are hard to interpret from the manuscript alone, and several conclusions rely on appendix plots without enough numerical summaries or statistical testing in the main text. Standard deviations in Table 1 are often large, so claims of decisive superiority should be phrased more cautiously.

Limitations and ethics are treated lightly. The conclusion mentions future work on stochastic shortest-path distance, but the paper should more explicitly discuss coverage assumptions, failure modes under partial observability/noisy observations, risks of using support-based distances in stochastic domains, and any ethical considerations for offline RL deployment.
